nodes.label: Annales
nodes.scope_note: Generations overlap and disagree. The founders’ exchange programme differs from Braudel’s duration, serial economic models and the 1988–1989 methodological reconsideration. Roster contexts include named resources, critics and collaborators, not a uniform membership list. Women’s history and Italian microstoria retain independent histories; their specific exchanges do not establish a single Annales origin.

nodes.label: Microhistory / everyday life
nodes.scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.

nodes.label: Environmental history
nodes.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

nodes.label: Gender & racial formation
nodes.scope_note: Scott’s gender analysis, Omi/Winant’s racial formation and Crenshaw’s legal critique are distinct projects. Historical studies of class, masculinity, caste and colonial categories extend and contest their terms. Productive feminist inheritance from Marxist history coexists with criticism; situated African arguments do not establish one continental gender system.

sources.title: Joan W. Scott: Gender as a category of historical analysis
sources.citation: Joan W. Scott, “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis,” American Historical Review 91, no. 5 (1986): 1053–75, especially 1059–60.

verification.note: Scanned pages 1059–60 checked for Marxist feminist approaches, British socialist-feminist debates, and Scott’s criticism of economic determination. This is her intervention, not a consensus account of all gender history. Additional primary pp. 1067–1068 checked in revision 1.25: Rosaldo and Foucault named, gender defined relationally, institutions and subjective identity distinguished, and universal psychoanalytic claims qualified. Full article remains unreviewed. Additional 2026-09-12 reading: complete printed pp. 1062–1066 through OCR of PDF indices 10–14. Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but criticizes universal binary antagonism and insufficient historical variability; she discusses Sally Alexander, de Lauretis and Riley and productively cites Derrida. These are Scott’s readings, not independent readings of every cited work. Original cited Lacanian collections and Alexander essay remain uncollated.
